title: Quantum mechanics I
tagline: Wavefunctions, operators and the hydrogen atom
summary: The experimental origins, the Schrödinger equation, piecewise potentials, the harmonic oscillator, the formal theory, angular momentum, hydrogen and spin.
overview: Quantum mechanics replaces the trajectory of a particle by a wavefunction, whose modulus squared is a probability density, and replaces dynamical quantities by operators. The Schrödinger equation is the equation of motion. Almost every exact solution an undergraduate meets is in this course: the free particle, the infinite and finite wells, the step, the harmonic oscillator and the hydrogen atom.

The first four chapters are the wave mechanics of one dimension, where the new ideas can be seen without angular momentum. The formal chapter then says what a state, an observable and a measurement are, so that angular momentum, hydrogen and spin are applications of a single structure rather than three separate tricks. Spin is introduced as an angular momentum that is not a function of position; the Stern–Gerlach experiment is the evidence.

Normalisation, boundary conditions and the difference between a stationary state and a wave packet are the points to be careful about. A stationary state has a time-independent probability density even though the wavefunction carries a phase e^{−iEt/ℏ}. Superpositions are what move.
outcomes: State the experimental evidence that classical mechanics fails at atomic scales, and the de Broglie relation.
Solve the time-independent Schrödinger equation for piecewise constant potentials and interpret the solutions.
Solve the harmonic oscillator with raising and lowering operators and with the differential equation.
Use Dirac notation, compute expectation values and uncertainties, and state the measurement postulate.
Add angular momenta in the cases needed for atoms, and use spherical harmonics at the level of their properties.
Solve the hydrogen atom for the energy levels and the angular part of the wavefunction, and describe spin-1/2.

chapters.title: Where the classical theory fails
chapters.summary: Black-body radiation, the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, Bohr’s atom and de Broglie waves.

chapters.title: The Schrödinger equation
chapters.summary: The wavefunction, probability, operators, expectation values and stationary states.

chapters.title: Piecewise potentials
chapters.summary: The infinite and finite wells, the step, the barrier and tunnelling.

chapters.title: The harmonic oscillator
chapters.summary: Series solution, Hermite polynomials, and the algebraic solution with a and a†.

chapters.title: States and observables
chapters.summary: Hilbert space, Dirac notation, compatible observables and the uncertainty principle.

chapters.title: Angular momentum
chapters.summary: Commutation relations, spherical harmonics, and the addition of two angular momenta.

chapters.title: The hydrogen atom
chapters.summary: Separation in spherical coordinates, energy levels, degeneracy and the radial wavefunctions.

chapters.title: Spin
chapters.summary: Spin 1/2, the Stern–Gerlach experiment, Pauli matrices and the magnetic moment.

history.title: Planck’s quantum
history.detail: On 14 December 1900 Planck presented a derivation of the black-body spectrum in which the energy of an oscillator is an integer multiple of hν.

history.title: Light quanta
history.detail: Einstein’s paper on the photoelectric effect treated light of frequency ν as quanta of energy hν, against the wave theory then in possession.

history.title: Bohr’s atom
history.detail: Bohr combined Rutherford’s nucleus with a quantisation condition and obtained the Balmer formula for hydrogen. The orbits were a temporary picture; the numbers survived.

history.title: Matter waves
history.detail: Louis de Broglie’s thesis assigned a wavelength h/p to a particle. Davisson and Germer, and independently G. P. Thomson, observed the diffraction of electrons in 1927.

history.title: Wave mechanics
history.detail: Schrödinger’s papers of 1926 introduced the wave equation and solved the hydrogen atom. Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics of 1925 is the same theory, as Schrödinger and Dirac showed.

history.title: Uncertainty
history.detail: Heisenberg’s uncertainty paper, and Born’s probability interpretation of the year before, fixed the reading of the wavefunction that this course uses.
